title: Identify the exact Android variant
summary: Record the full model code, region or carrier, build number, and bootloader state before choosing a support path.
scope: Android phones and tablets; Settings labels vary by manufacturer and software release.
prerequisites: Owner authorization; access to Settings or device label; a second device for source research.
steps: Open Settings → About phone/tablet and copy the model number and build details exactly.
Compare the full code with the manufacturer support page; the retail name alone is not enough.
Check carrier, region, chipset, and bootloader state before matching firmware or drivers.
Stop if the code or source does not match; do not cross-flash a similar model.
risks: Do not post serial numbers, IMEI, account identifiers, or diagnostic dumps publicly. Firmware mismatch can wipe data or prevent boot.

title: Back up before repair or restore
summary: Confirm the owner’s backup and account access before resets, bootloader changes, or firmware operations.
scope: Any Android device; backup features depend on device, account, region, and app.
prerequisites: Owner consent and account access; stable Wi-Fi or computer; adequate battery.
steps: Verify the latest cloud or local backup date and ensure photos, messages, and authenticator access are covered.
Export files not included in backup; verify a sample can be opened on another device.
Confirm the owner knows the Google account and recovery method currently associated with the phone.
Only then follow the exact manufacturer instructions for the identified model.
risks: Factory reset, unlocking, restore, and some firmware actions erase data. A backup may not include every app or protected item.

title: ADB, Fastboot, and USB driver basics
summary: Understand the difference between Android Debug Bridge and bootloader Fastboot, then use Google Platform-Tools and device-vendor driver instructions.
scope: ADB works on supported running Android devices; Fastboot availability and unlock policy are device-specific.
prerequisites: Trusted computer, data-capable USB cable, exact model, owner consent, and verified backup for write operations.
steps: Download Platform-Tools from Google Android Developers, not a repackaged installer.
Install the OEM driver on Windows when required; macOS and Linux typically use their USB device rules.
Enable USB debugging only for a task that needs it and approve the computer on the device.
Use read-only identification first; do not issue erase, unlock, flash, or partition-write operations without exact official instructions.
risks: Unlocking commonly wipes data. Fastboot commands and images are not universal; an incorrect write may brick or erase the device.

title: Google Pixel factory images and browser flashing
summary: Use Google device-specific notes and supported factory image or Android Flash Tool workflow for eligible Pixel models.
scope: Only Pixel devices and builds explicitly listed by Google. Carrier and regional variants can differ.
prerequisites: Exact Pixel model and build, current backup, charged battery, reliable USB cable, compatible browser/computer, and required OEM unlock setting.
steps: Match the device model and carrier/region on Google’s page before selecting an image.
Read image-specific notes and whether the action wipes data or requires bootloader unlocking.
Prefer the official Android Flash Tool when the selected model and workflow are supported.
Follow Google instructions for that build; stop on any mismatch or unexplained tool error.
risks: A factory image restore may erase data. Bootloader unlocking weakens protection while enabled; relocking with the wrong image can make the phone unusable.

title: Android Flash Tool: safe preflight
summary: Google’s web flasher supports specified Pixel devices and builds; check the compatibility list and instructions before connecting.
scope: Only supported Google Pixel devices and listed builds; not a general Android flashing tool.
prerequisites: Supported Pixel, current backup, compatible desktop browser, data USB cable, battery charge, and owner authorization.
steps: Use the official Android Flash Tool site and its device selector.
Read the displayed build, wipe, and bootloader requirements before starting.
Confirm a backup and account credentials; disconnect unrelated devices.
Follow the supported on-screen flow and stop if the device identity is unexpected.
risks: Flashing can erase data and change bootloader state. Do not use the Pixel tool with other manufacturers or unlisted variants.

title: Samsung updates, backups, and recovery
summary: Start with Samsung Support and Smart Switch for supported backup, transfer, and update workflows; verify model and region first.
scope: Samsung Galaxy devices for which Samsung documents the selected feature.
prerequisites: Exact model and country, Samsung account where needed, backup destination, stable USB/Wi-Fi connection.
steps: Open the device country-specific Samsung support page and identify the exact model code.
Use Smart Switch only for its documented transfer, backup, or supported update feature.
For boot or restore errors, record the displayed error and follow Samsung model-specific support.
Contact Samsung service when official recovery does not cover the case; do not use a random firmware mirror.
risks: Updates and restores can fail or erase data. Odin is not presented here as an official Samsung consumer download or universal service method.

title: Factory Reset Protection: owner recovery
summary: FRP is an ownership safeguard. After a protected reset, the owner should use a previously synced account or recover that account through Google or the manufacturer.
scope: Android devices with Google device protection; screens depend on vendor and release.
prerequisites: Owner or authorized technician must have the owner present and proof of lawful ownership when required.
steps: Ask the owner to enter an account previously synced to the device before reset.
If credentials are forgotten, complete Google Account recovery from a trusted device.
For second-hand devices, ask the prior owner to remove their account through the supported process or contact the manufacturer with proof of purchase.
Do not accept bypass claims or unofficial services asking for credentials or remote access.
risks: Waiting periods, account checks, and vendor procedures may apply. This guide intentionally provides no bypass steps.

title: Android bootloop: non-destructive triage
summary: Collect symptoms and try manufacturer-supported, non-erasing recovery steps before any reset or firmware operation.
scope: General triage only; button sequences and recovery menus vary by exact model.
prerequisites: Owner approval, exact model, known recent changes, and backup status check.
steps: Record whether the device reaches the logo, recovery, or bootloader; note recent updates, drops, liquid exposure, or accessory changes.
Disconnect accessories and use the manufacturer documented forced restart for the exact model.
If recovery appears, read the selected menu carefully; avoid Wipe data/Factory reset unless the owner approved data loss.
Consult manufacturer service or authorized repair before a firmware write.
risks: A factory reset erases data. Repeated failed boots may indicate hardware failure; do not keep flashing to diagnose it.

title: Qualcomm, MediaTek, and Unisoc compatibility
summary: Chipset names alone do not establish compatibility. Use the manufacturer model-specific service path and documented host drivers.
scope: Devices with a supported service or developer interface; access and methods vary widely.
prerequisites: Exact model/board code, vendor documentation, lawful ownership, current backup, documented tool version.
steps: Identify the complete model and board/region from manufacturer information, not a guessed chipset.
Find the official support or developer tool for that exact product and region.
Install drivers only from the OS or device manufacturer; avoid repacked driver bundles.
Stop if a tool asks for unknown loaders, authorization tokens, or unverified firmware.
risks: Low-level tools can read or write protected partitions and cause permanent loss. This catalogue does not imply chipset support.

title: Back up an iPhone before updating or restoring
summary: Check the latest iCloud or computer backup and confirm the owner can access their Apple Account before restoring.
scope: iPhone and iPad; menu labels and backup availability depend on OS, region, and account settings.
prerequisites: Owner consent, Apple Account access, adequate storage, stable Wi-Fi or trusted computer.
steps: Check the last successful iCloud backup or make an encrypted computer backup where appropriate.
Verify photos and important files are synced or copied separately.
Confirm the owner knows the Apple Account and has access to a trusted phone number or recovery contact.
Then follow Apple model-specific update or restore guidance.
risks: Restore erases device contents. Some data may not be included in a backup or may require the original account after setup.

title: iPhone recovery mode: update versus restore
summary: Apple recovery mode can offer Update or Restore on a computer. Try Update when offered; Restore erases the device.
scope: iPhone and iPad models covered by Apple recovery-mode instructions.
prerequisites: Current computer software, trusted cable, owner approval, backup check, reliable USB connection.
steps: Identify the iPhone model so you use the correct Apple button sequence.
Connect to Finder or Apple Devices/iTunes as Apple instructions specify.
Choose Update first when offered and appropriate; choose Restore only after the owner accepts data erasure.
If recovery fails or repeats, record the error and follow Apple service guidance.
risks: Restore erases content and does not remove Activation Lock. Never use a third-party claim to bypass account ownership.

title: DFU, diagnostics, and restore errors
summary: DFU is a lower-level device update state sometimes used during service, but steps are model-specific. Use Apple published recovery and diagnostics resources first.
scope: Only procedures documented for the exact Apple model; no universal DFU sequence is asserted here.
prerequisites: Exact model, backup status, current Apple software, stable power/USB, and owner consent.
steps: Write down the Apple device model and complete error shown by Finder or Apple Devices.
Check Apple current recovery and repair guidance before changing modes.
Run Apple diagnostics when available and record its reference code for support.
Escalate repeated restore failure to Apple or an authorized service provider.
risks: A restore can erase data; repeated DFU attempts or unofficial firmware can complicate diagnosis. DFU does not defeat Activation Lock.

title: Apple Account recovery and Activation Lock
summary: The original owner must recover their Apple Account or remove the device from that account. Apple can review eligible proof-of-purchase requests.
scope: Apple Account and Activation Lock cases; eligibility and steps are determined by Apple.
prerequisites: Original account owner or valid proof of purchase; do not share passwords or one-time codes with a repairer.
steps: Use Apple iforgot from a trusted browser to recover account access.
For a used device, ask the previous owner to remove it from their account using Apple supported process.
If the owner has proof of purchase, submit the official Activation Lock support request.
Decline third-party unlock offers and do not give anyone the account password or verification code.
risks: Recovery can take time and Apple may require proof of ownership. A reset or DFU restore does not remove Activation Lock.

title: Jailbreak concepts and compatibility checks
summary: A jailbreak changes iOS security controls. Compatibility must be checked against exact device, processor, OS build, and maintained project documentation.
scope: Educational overview only; TechNex Labs does not assert current jailbreak compatibility.
prerequisites: A device the learner owns, verified backup, understanding of security tradeoffs, primary-source release notes.
steps: Record the exact iPhone model and full iOS build.
Read a project compatibility table and release notes; do not rely on a generic model-family claim.
Check whether the project is maintained and transparent about risks before considering it.
Avoid unknown configuration profiles, unsigned downloads, and tools promising Activation Lock removal.
risks: Jailbreaking can reduce security, affect support, expose data, and cause boot/update problems. No ownership bypass is supported.

title: Cybersecurity learning path for beginners
summary: Build fundamentals before using security tools: operating systems, networking, web architecture, and clear note-taking.
scope: Self-study on your own computer and isolated practice environments.
prerequisites: Personal computer, basic command-line familiarity, and commitment to test only authorized systems.
steps: Learn files, permissions, processes, shells, and package managers on a system you own.
Study IP addressing, DNS, HTTP, TLS, routing, and basic packet capture.
Learn how web requests, sessions, authentication, and databases work.
Then use intentionally vulnerable labs and document findings with evidence and remediation.
risks: A scanner or test can disrupt a service. Never scan public IPs, networks, or accounts without explicit authorization.

title: Web security practice in safe labs
summary: Use intentionally vulnerable training labs and OWASP guidance to learn controlled testing and defensive fixes.
scope: PortSwigger Web Security Academy labs, local toy apps, or systems with written authorization.
prerequisites: Read each lab scope and rules; use a separate test browser/profile and never enter real credentials.
steps: Start with the Academy learning path and its dedicated lab targets.
Reproduce a finding only within the assigned lab and note the request, impact, and fix.
Use the OWASP Testing Guide as a methodology reference and validate fixes in your own application.
Stop when a target is outside the lab boundary or an instruction is unclear.
risks: Do not apply lab techniques to third-party services. Report real issues privately through the owner disclosure channel.

title: Network inventory with Nmap in an owned lab
summary: Use Nmap official documentation to inventory a host or isolated lab you administer; understand scope and rate before scanning.
scope: Loopback, a private lab network you control, or explicitly authorized assets only.
prerequisites: Written scope, test window, target list, permission to send probes, and a record of asset ownership.
steps: Read the Nmap reference guide and understand host discovery and scan impact.
Begin with one lab host you own and document target and time window.
Use conservative defaults; avoid scripts or broad scans until the lab owner approves them.
Save results locally, remove sensitive data, and confirm unexpected services with the asset owner.
risks: Scanning can trigger alerts or degrade fragile systems. Never scan public or workplace networks without explicit authorization.

title: Learn packet analysis with Wireshark
summary: Practice reading protocol metadata from a sample capture or your own lab traffic and protect private data in packet files.
scope: Sample captures, loopback, or traffic you are explicitly allowed to inspect.
prerequisites: Wireshark from its official site, a sample capture, or authorization from network owner.
steps: Start with the official User Guide and learn capture/display filter concepts.
Use public sample captures or a local toy service; avoid collecting other people traffic.
Identify DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP metadata and write down what a packet can and cannot prove.
Remove secrets and personal data before sharing any capture file.
risks: Captures may contain credentials, identifiers, or private communications. Capture only authorized traffic and protect the output.

title: Password security and offline auditing
summary: Learn password policy and hash concepts with synthetic sample hashes in a local lab; never test accounts without authorization.
scope: Synthetic lab data or systems and hashes you own and are authorized to assess.
prerequisites: Isolated lab, synthetic accounts, written scope, secure storage for results, remediation plan.
steps: Understand password managers, MFA, rate limiting, and modern password hashing before using an auditor.
Generate toy test data locally; never download or reuse real credential dumps.
Run only a tool documented test mode against the lab data.
Delete test secrets and recommend unique passphrases, MFA, and approved breached-password checks.
risks: Hash or password material is highly sensitive. Do not collect, publish, or attempt to crack real users credentials without explicit authorization.

title: Responsible disclosure and test authorization
summary: Define written scope, allowed methods, time windows, data handling, and a private reporting channel before any security test.
scope: Programs and systems whose owner provided explicit authorization.
prerequisites: Written permission, exact asset list, and contact details for incident escalation.
steps: Record owner, exact hosts/apps, dates, prohibited actions, and data limits.
Use test accounts and non-destructive checks unless scope explicitly permits more.
Stop on access to real user data, service disruption, or scope uncertainty.
Report a concise reproduction, impact, timestamps, and remediation privately to owner.
risks: Good intent does not replace authorization. Laws and program rules differ; remain within written scope.
